title: Audit three release branches for missing fixes
summary: Security releases every quarter, three supported versions, and nobody is sure which branch has which fix. Build the audit that answers it, then backport what is missing.
mental_model: Reachability (`--contains`) and content (`git cherry`) answer different questions. For backport auditing you want content, because every backport has a different sha from the fix it copies.

commit.message: SECURITY: bound the parser input size

setup.run: sh -c 'git cherry-pick -x $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="parser input size" main)'

steps.title: See the shape of the problem
steps.why: Two security fixes on main, three supported releases, and backports done at different times by different people. No amount of reading the graph tells you reliably what is missing.
steps.expect: Three release branches at different states.

steps.title: Watch --contains give the wrong answer
steps.why: The fixes were cherry-picked, so the copies have different shas. `--contains` reports only main, and would have you re-backporting fixes that are already there.
steps.expect: Only main for both — despite two branches already having the fixes.

verify.label: reachability sees only main, because backports change the sha

steps.title: Ask the content question per branch
steps.why: `git cherry <upstream> <head>` compares patch ids. A `+` means the commit on the release branch has no equivalent upstream; the reverse direction is what tells you what the branch is missing.
steps.expect: 1.2 is missing nothing security-related, 1.1 is missing the parser fix, 1.0 is missing both.

verify.label: the oldest release is missing commits by content

steps.title: Build the audit as a loop
steps.why: One command per branch, filtered to the commits that matter. This is the report you run before every security release, and it takes a second.
commands: sh -c 'for b in release/1.0 release/1.1 release/1.2; do echo "== $b"; git cherry $b main | grep "^+" | while read _ sha; do git log -1 --format="   MISSING %h %s" $sha; done | grep SECURITY || echo "   all security fixes present"; done'
steps.expect: A per-branch list naming exactly which security commits are absent.

steps.title: Backport what 1.1 is missing
steps.why: One fix, one cherry-pick, `-x` for provenance. The audit told you precisely what to run, which is the difference between a backport process and guesswork.

actions.run: sh -c 'git cherry-pick -x $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="parser input size" main)'

verify.label: release/1.1 now has the parser fix

steps.title: Backport both to the oldest release
steps.why: Order matters when fixes touch the same file; here they do not, so both apply cleanly. Cherry-picking oldest-first keeps the branch history in the same order as main.

actions.run: sh -c 'git cherry-pick -x $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="parser input size" main)'

verify.label: the oldest release has the auth fix

steps.title: Re-run the audit and prove it is clean
steps.why: Every branch reports no missing security commits. Because the check is by content, it stays correct however the backports were made — cherry-picked, hand-applied, or merged.
commands: sh -c 'for b in release/1.0 release/1.1 release/1.2; do printf "%-14s " $b; git cherry $b main | grep "^+" | while read _ sha; do git log -1 --format=%s $sha; done | grep -c SECURITY | sed "s/^/missing security fixes: /"; done'

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git cherry release/1.0 main | grep "^+" | while read _ s; do git log -1 --format=%s $s; done | grep -c SECURITY'
verify.label: no security fix is missing from the oldest release
release/1.0 received the auth fix
verify.hint: audit with git cherry, then cherry-pick -x what is missing

verify.label: release/1.1 received the fix it was missing
the backports record where they came from
verify.hint: -x is what makes the audit trail readable later

pitfalls: `git branch --contains` is the wrong tool for backport auditing: every cherry-pick has a new sha, so it reports nothing.
`git cherry` compares patch ids, which survive cherry-picks and rebases — but a fix adapted during the backport has a different patch id and shows as missing.
Argument order is `git cherry <upstream> <head>`: the `+` lines are commits in head that have no equivalent upstream. Swap them to ask the other direction.
Cherry-pick oldest-first when backporting several commits, or later fixes conflict against a file the earlier fix has not touched yet.
Record backports with `-x`. Without it, a future audit cannot distinguish a backport from an independent change that happens to look similar.
